title: Microbes: tiny living beings on your hands, in soil and in curd

summary.text: Three slices of boiled potato look clean. Touch one with your fingers and one with a pinch of soil, and in a few days both grow coloured spots. Each spot is a crowd of microbes, living beings too small to see, that grew from a few. Microbes live on your hands, in the soil of a flower pot, in the air, and by the million in a spoon of curd. In this unit you grow them where you can see them, smell what soil microbes make, and use them to set curd.
summary.art: Three clear plastic boxes in a row on a kitchen shelf, each holding a slice of boiled potato: one covered in coloured spots, one with a few spots in the shape of fingertips, one almost clean.

intro.hook: Look closely at your palm. You can see skin and lines, and nothing else. Yet thousands of tiny living beings are on it right now. How could we find out if that is true?
intro.text: Some living beings are far too small to see with our eyes alone. They are called microbes. One microbe is too small to see, but a microbe can split into two, and two into four. On food, in a warm place, a few microbes can become millions in a day or two. Millions together make a spot we can see. So if we give the microbes on our hands some food, we can watch them grow.
intro.art: A child's open palm held up to a window, with a dotted circle zooming in to show many tiny round and rod-shaped microbes on the skin.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a microbe is: a living being too small to see with our eyes alone.
By the end I can name places where microbes live, such as hands, soil, air, curd and inside my tummy.
By the end I can grow microbes on potato slices, count the spots, and say that each spot grew from a few microbes that multiplied.
By the end I can say how curd is made: curd bacteria eat the sugar in milk and make the milk thick and sour.
By the end I can say that most microbes are harmless or helpful, and only a few make us ill.
By the end I can do a fair test with three slices, and say what I think, what I saw and why.

terms.meaning: A microbe is a living being too small to see with our eyes alone. Another name for microbes is microorganisms.
terms.example: Thousands of microbes live on your hands, and millions live in one spoon of curd.
terms.art: A spoon of curd with a zoom circle showing many tiny rod-shaped bacteria inside.

terms.meaning: Bacteria are one big group of microbes. Each one is a single tiny cell. One of them is called a bacterium.
terms.example: The bacteria in curd turn milk into curd overnight.
terms.art: Many tiny rod and ball shapes, coloured pink and blue, as seen through a microscope.

terms.meaning: A fungus is a living being that grows by spreading thin threads. The threads feed on whatever they grow on. Mushrooms, mould and yeast are fungi.
terms.example: A fluffy green patch on an old orange is a fungus called a mould.
terms.art: A mushroom, a slice of bread with fuzzy green mould, and a pinch of yeast, side by side.

terms.meaning: Mould is a fungus that grows as fuzzy patches on old food. The fuzz is made of very thin threads.
terms.example: White or green fuzz on old bread is mould.
terms.art: An old slice of bread with round green and white fuzzy patches.

terms.meaning: To multiply means to become many. A bacterium multiplies by splitting into two new bacteria.
terms.example: One bacterium splits into 2, then 4, then 8, then 16.
terms.art: One small round cell splitting into two, then four, then eight, drawn in a row.

terms.meaning: A colony is a spot of microbes that all grew from one or a few. A colony holds millions of microbes, so we can see the colony even though each microbe is too small to see.
terms.example: Each coloured spot on the potato slice is one colony.
terms.art: A potato slice with round spots of yellow, white and orange, and a zoom circle on one spot showing it is made of countless tiny cells.

terms.meaning: A starter is a little curd added to warm milk to turn the milk into curd. The starter carries the curd bacteria.
terms.example: Many families save one spoon of today's curd as the starter for tomorrow's curd.
terms.art: A hand dropping one spoon of white curd into a steel vessel of warm milk.

terms.meaning: A germ is one of the few microbes that can make humans and other animals ill. Most microbes are not germs.
terms.example: The microbe that gives you a cold is a germ. The bacteria in curd are not germs.
terms.art: A big crowd of friendly-looking microbes, with just two or three grumpy ones at the edge.

terms.meaning: A microscope is a tool with special lenses that makes tiny things look much bigger. With a microscope we can see single microbes.
terms.example: Scientists look at a drop of curd under a microscope and see the bacteria.
terms.art: A girl looking into a microscope on a table, with a drop of curd on a glass slide under the lens.

explanations.context: This card says what a microbe is, and how small microbes are.
explanations.definition: A microbe is a living being too small to see with our eyes alone. Most microbes are a single cell.
explanations.description: Microbes are tiny. About a thousand bacteria in a line would just reach across a mustard seed. We cannot see one, but we can see a crowd of millions, like a spot on old food. Bacteria and tiny fungi such as yeast are microbes, and some scientists count viruses too.
examples: The bacteria that turn milk into curd.
The yeast that makes bread dough puff up.
The mould that grows fuzzy spots on an old chapati.
explanations.art: A mustard seed on a fingertip, with a line of tiny bacteria drawn across the seed from one side to the other.

explanations.context: This card is about where microbes live. In the Three Potato Slices experiment, the slices touched by fingers and by soil grew spots.
explanations.definition: Microbes live almost everywhere on Earth: on our skin, inside our bodies, in soil, water and air, and on everything we touch.
explanations.description: Your hands carry thousands of microbes, even when they look clean. One teaspoon of rich soil can hold about as many bacteria as there are people in India. Microbes float in the air on dust, and live in the sea, in hot springs and deep in ice. Most of the microbes in your body live in your tummy.
examples: In the Three Potato Slices experiment, spots grew on the slice your fingers touched.
The soil slice grew the most spots, because soil is packed with microbes.
Even a slice that nobody touched can grow a spot, from microbes that floated in on the air.
explanations.art: A cut-away picture of a flat: a child's hand, a flower pot, a katori of curd and the air near a window, each with a zoom circle full of tiny microbes.

explanations.context: This card explains why the spots on the potato slices appeared and grew.
explanations.definition: A bacterium grows a little, then splits into two bacteria. Each of those splits again. This is how microbes multiply.
explanations.description: In a warm place with food, some bacteria split about every half hour. One becomes 2, then 4, then 8, and by the next day there can be millions. That crowd is a colony, big enough to see. Each spot on your potato slice started as one or a few microbes that landed there.
examples: A shiny yellow or white spot on the potato is a colony of bacteria.
A fuzzy patch is mould, a fungus that grows threads.
Spots grow faster in a warm kitchen than in a cold room.
explanations.art: Four panels: one tiny cell on a potato slice, then two, then four, then a round spot you can see, with a clock in each panel.

explanations.context: This card explains how a spoon of curd turns milk into curd.
explanations.definition: Curd bacteria eat the sugar in milk and make an acid. The acid makes the milk thick and sour. That thick, sour milk is curd.
explanations.description: Milk has a sugar in it, though it does not taste very sweet. A spoon of curd adds millions of curd bacteria to warm milk. They eat the sugar, multiply, and make an acid, and the acid makes the milk proteins clump into soft curd. In the fridge they work slowly, so set curd keeps longer there.
examples: Thayir, mosaru, perugu, dahi and doi are names for curd in different parts of India.
Mishti doi in West Bengal is set with curd bacteria, after the milk is sweetened.
Moru, or buttermilk, is curd mixed with water.
explanations.art: A steel vessel of warm milk with a spoon of curd going in, a clock, and the same vessel next morning full of thick white curd.

explanations.context: This card is about what microbes do, and what scientists argue about.
explanations.description: Microbes sense, decide and act. A bacterium senses food in the water and swims towards it. Bacteria also give out tiny amounts of chemicals, and by sensing these they can tell how many of their own kind are near. Scientists still argue about what to call this.
examples: Bacteria swim towards sugar and away from things that harm them.
Some sea bacteria glow only when enough of them are together, as Bonnie Bassler and other scientists have shown.
Mould threads grow towards food and away from dry places.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who study single cells
perspectives.explanation: Microbes sense their world, remember a little of what just happened, and choose what to do next. This is a simple kind of thinking, done by one cell without a brain.
Microbes react to chemicals the way a thermostat reacts to heat. These are automatic responses, and calling them thinking says too much.

explanations.art: A single bacterium with a tail, swimming towards a sugar crystal, with small arrows showing the sugar spreading in the water.

explanations.concept: Most microbes are harmless or helpful
explanations.context: This card is about which microbes help us and which ones can make us ill.
explanations.definition: Most microbes do not make anyone ill. Many are helpful. Only a few, called germs, can make humans and other animals ill.
explanations.description: Microbes in soil break dead leaves into new soil, and microbes in your tummy help you digest food. Curd bacteria and the microbes in idli batter make food we love. Tiny living beings in the sea, many of them microbes, make about half the oxygen we breathe. A few microbes are germs, and washing hands with soap removes most of them before they get inside us.
examples: The microbes on your skin are mostly harmless, and some of them help keep germs away.
The microbes that cause a cold or a tummy upset are germs.
explanations.art: A big crowd of smiling microbes doing jobs, one making curd, one breaking a dead leaf, one in a tummy, and just two grumpy germs at the edge.

agreed.text: Microbes live almost everywhere on Earth, from our skin to hot springs and deep ice.
agreed.evidence: Scientists take samples from soil, air, water, skin and ice, and grow or look at the microbes in them. They find microbes in almost every sample.
Milk with a spoon of living curd sets into curd. Milk with nothing added does not set into smooth curd. Under a microscope, curd is full of bacteria.

agreed.text: A spot that grows on food is a colony of millions of microbes.
agreed.evidence: Scientists look at a tiny bit of a spot under a microscope and see it is packed with cells. Spread on fresh food, a bit of one spot grows into new spots of the same kind.

challenging.claim: A hand that looks clean has nothing living on it.
challenging.who: A common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: We cannot see anything on a clean-looking hand.
challenging.against: In the Three Potato Slices experiment, the slice touched by fingers grew spots, and the slice nobody touched grew the fewest. Microbes were on the fingers, too small to see.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that clean-looking means nothing living is there.

challenging.claim: All microbes are bad and make us ill.
challenging.who: A common idea, from advertisements for cleaning liquids
challenging.for: Some microbes, called germs, do make people ill.
challenging.against: Most microbes are harmless or helpful. Curd, idli batter and soil all depend on microbes, and the microbes in our tummy help us digest food.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that every microbe is a germ.

challenging.claim: Spots and rot come out of the food itself.
challenging.who: Many people, until about 160 years ago
challenging.for: Food left out seems to grow spots on its own.
challenging.against: In the 1860s, Louis Pasteur showed that boiled soup kept away from dust and air did not spoil. The spots come from microbes that land on the food.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where spots on food come from.

challenging.claim: Children who meet many kinds of harmless microbes are less likely to get some allergies.
challenging.for: Children who grow up on farms, around animals and soil, get some allergies less often.
challenging.against: Scientists are still working out why, and which microbes matter. Washing hands with soap is still needed to keep germs away.
challenging.context: This card is about an idea scientists are still testing.

big_questions.q: You cannot see a microbe. So how do you know microbes are there?
big_questions.hint: Think about the spots that grew on the potato slices, and the milk that turned into curd overnight.

big_questions.q: The spots grew on the potato. Did they come from the potato, or from somewhere else?
big_questions.hint: In the Three Potato Slices experiment, nobody touched one of the slices. How many spots did that slice grow?

big_questions.q: Millions of microbes live on you and inside you. Are they part of you, or are they guests?
big_questions.hint: Think about the microbes in your tummy that help you digest food.

big_questions.q: Microbes lived on Earth for billions of years before there were any animals. Whose planet is Earth?
big_questions.hint: Think about who was here first, and who is here in the biggest numbers.

how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, people made curd, idli batter and bread with the help of microbes, without knowing microbes were there. In 1676, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a cloth seller in the Netherlands, looked through tiny lenses he made himself. In drops of water, he saw tiny living beings swimming about. Later he saw them in the white stuff scraped from his own teeth. Still, most people believed that rot and spots came out of the food itself. In about 1860, Louis Pasteur in France boiled soup in glass flasks with long, bent necks. Dust and microbes from the air got stuck in the bend, and the soup stayed fresh. When he broke a neck off, dust fell in, and the soup went cloudy and bad. So the spoiling came from microbes that arrived from outside. In 1881, Fanny Hesse, who worked in a laboratory in Germany, suggested a jelly called agar for growing microbes. She knew agar from her kitchen. Scientists still grow microbes on agar today.
how_we_found_out.who: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, Louis Pasteur and Fanny Hesse
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That rot and spots on food come out of the food itself, and not from microbes that land on it.

story.title: Ammamma's Spoon of Curd
story.note: Nila, Kannan and Ammamma are made up. The facts are real: curd bacteria set warm milk overnight, soil bacteria make much of the earthy smell after rain, and boiled potato slices grow spots from microbes that touch them.
text: It was the last week of the rains in Kozhikode. Nila was seven. Every night after dinner, she watched her Ammamma, her grandmother, make curd for the next day.

Ammamma always did the same thing. She warmed the milk until it felt as warm as a bath. She poured it into the clay pot. Then she took one spoon of curd from the old bowl and stirred it in. She put the lid on and set the pot on the shelf above the stove.
'Ammamma, why do you always add that spoon?' Nila asked. 'We have so much curd already.'
'That spoon holds the workers,' said Ammamma. 'Without them, the milk stays milk.'
Nila looked into the old bowl. She saw white curd and nothing else. 'There are no workers in there,' she said. 'It is just curd.'
Her little brother Kannan, who was five, came to look too. 'Is it magic?' he asked.

Ammamma laughed. 'Not magic. Tiny living beings, called bacteria. They are too small for your eyes. One spoon of curd holds millions of them. Tonight they will eat the sugar in the warm milk. They will make the milk sour and thick. And they will split into two, and two, and two again, until the whole pot is full of them.'
Nila did not believe her. In the morning, she ran to the shelf before brushing her teeth. She lifted the lid. The pot was full of thick, white curd. She tipped it a little. The curd did not move.
'They did it,' she whispered.
That afternoon it rained again. Ammamma opened the balcony door, and a smell came in from the wet pots of tulsi and chilli plants. It was a deep, earthy smell. Nila loved it.

'Do you know who makes that smell?' asked Ammamma. 'More tiny workers. Bacteria in the soil make that smell, and the rain lifts the smell into the air. One teaspoon of rich soil can hold about as many bacteria as there are people in India.'
Nila looked at her own hands. 'Are there bacteria on me too?'
'Thousands,' said Ammamma. 'On your hands, in your mouth, in your tummy. Most of them are harmless, and many help you. A few can make you ill. That is why we wash with soap before we eat.'
Nila frowned. 'But how can I know they are there, if I cannot see them?'
Ammamma thought for a moment. 'You cannot see one bacterium,' she said. 'But you can see a crowd of millions. Give them food and a warm place, and wait.'

So that evening, Ammamma boiled a potato. She cut three thick slices with a clean knife. She put each slice in its own little box. Nila pressed her fingertips on the first slice. Kannan sprinkled a pinch of soil from the tulsi pot on the second. Nobody touched the third. Ammamma closed all three boxes.

On the first day, all three slices looked the same. On the second day, tiny shiny dots appeared on the soil slice. On the third day, the soil slice had yellow spots, white spots and grey fuzz. Nila's slice had small round spots, just where her fingertips had pressed. The third slice had only one tiny spot.
'Those spots are crowds,' Nila told Kannan. 'Each spot grew from a few bacteria, too small to see. Mine came from my fingers.'
'Then why does the third one have a spot?' asked Kannan. 'Nobody touched it.'
Nila thought about it. 'Maybe one floated in on the air before Ammamma closed the box,' she said. 'They are in the air too.'
Ammamma smiled. She put the three boxes in a bag, tied it shut and put it in the bin. Then Nila and Kannan washed their hands with soap, singing all the way through one song.
That night, Nila watched Ammamma add the spoon of curd to the warm milk. This time Nila said it first. 'The workers are going in.'
story.epiphany: Nila saw that her clean-looking fingers had carried living beings all along. She could not see one microbe, but she could see the spot that a few of them grew into.
ask: Why did Ammamma add one spoon of old curd to the warm milk?
Why did the soil slice grow the most spots?
The third slice grew one spot, though nobody touched it. Where could that spot have come from?
art: Ammamma stirring a spoon of curd into a clay pot of warm milk in a Kerala kitchen at night, Nila and Kannan watching.
Nila lifting the lid of the clay pot in the morning to find thick white curd.
Three small boxes with potato slices: one spotty with soil, one with fingertip spots, one almost clean, and Nila pointing at them for Kannan.

experiments.title: Three Potato Slices: where do the spots come from?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put three slices of boiled potato in three closed boxes. Your fingers touch one slice, a pinch of soil touches another, and nothing touches the third. Over three or four days you count the spots that grow. This shows where microbes were hiding.
experiments.question: Our fingers and the soil in a flower pot look like they have nothing alive on them. Do they carry microbes we cannot see?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which slice will grow the most spots: the finger slice, the soil slice, or the slice nobody touched? Which will grow the fewest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three slices come from the same potato, are the same thickness, sit in the same kind of box, in the same place, for the same number of days. Only one thing is different: what touched each slice. So if the slices grow different numbers of spots, what touched them made the difference. The slice nobody touched shows what grows from the air alone.

materials.item: one potato, boiled with the skin on and cooled until you can hold it
a clean knife, rinsed in just-boiled water (for the grown-up)
three small clear plastic boxes with lids, or three clear zip bags (or three steel katoris, each covered with a plate)
a pinch of soil from a flower pot (or a pinch of dust swept from the balcony floor)
three paper labels and a pen: Fingers, Soil, Nobody
a magnifying glass, or the zoom on a phone camera, if you have one

experiments.safety: Keep the boxes closed once the spots grow. Never sniff or open them wide, because mould spores can upset breathing, especially for anyone with asthma. A grown-up cuts the potato and throws away the boxes, tied in a bag. Wash hands with soap after touching the soil and after the test.

schedule.what: Cut three slices. Guess which slice will grow the most spots. Touch one slice with unwashed fingers and one with a pinch of soil. Close all three boxes and put them in a warm, dark place. Wash hands.
Look through the lids. Count any spots on each slice and write the numbers down.
Count the spots again. Look for colours and fuzz.
Count one last time. Draw the slices. Say what you think, what you saw and why. A grown-up throws the closed boxes away in a tied bag.

experiments.record: Draw the three slices on day 4, with every spot in its colour. Write the number of spots under each slice.

flow.do: Take the potato that was boiled with its skin on and cooled until you can hold it. Show it to your child.
flow.say: Look at this boiled potato. Boiling killed almost every microbe inside the potato. Can you see anything living on it?
flow.kid: Look at the boiled potato. Can you see anything living on it?

ask.q: Do you see anything living on the potato?
good: No, it looks clean.
Nothing, just potato.

flow.parent: Boiling takes about 20 minutes, so boil the potato earlier, or use one left from a meal. Keep it aside before anyone touches it. Boiling kills almost all microbes, so the slices start nearly empty of life.

flow.do: 1. Rinse the knife in just-boiled water. 2. Cut three slices, each about as thick as your finger. 3. Put one slice in each box straight away. 4. Close the box labelled Nobody at once.
flow.say: I am cutting three slices. This one goes straight into the Nobody box, and the lid goes on now.
flow.kid: Watch the grown-up cut three slices. The Nobody box gets closed at once.
flow.parent: Thick slices dry out less, so they grow spots better. Don't touch the cut faces with your fingers. If you use katoris, cover each with a plate.

flow.do: Tell your child the plan. Ask for a guess and a reason for each slice. Write the guesses on a paper.
flow.say: You will touch one slice with your fingers. You will sprinkle soil on another. Nobody touches the third. Which one will grow the most spots? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Your fingers touch one slice. Soil goes on one slice. Nobody touches the third. Which grows the most spots? Why?

ask.q: Which slice will grow the most spots, and why?
good: The soil one, because soil is dirty.
The finger one, because I played outside.
None of them, because my hands are clean.

flow.parent: Every guess is fine, as long as your child gives a reason. Don't say what you expect.

flow.do: 1. Your child presses three unwashed fingertips gently on the slice in the Fingers box. 2. Your child sprinkles a tiny pinch of soil on the slice in the Soil box. 3. Close both lids. 4. Wash hands with soap.
flow.say: Press three fingertips gently on this slice. Don't wash first. Now sprinkle a tiny pinch of soil on that one. Lids on, then we wash hands.
flow.kid: Press three fingers on the Fingers slice. Sprinkle a little soil on the Soil slice. Close the lids. Wash your hands with soap.
flow.parent: Use hands that have been playing, not hands just washed. A tiny pinch of soil is enough. Too much soil hides the spots.

flow.do: 1. Put the three boxes side by side in a warm, dark place, such as a kitchen shelf or inside a cupboard. 2. Leave them closed.
flow.say: Microbes grow best where it is warm and dark. We leave the boxes here, closed, and look again in two days.
flow.kid: Put the boxes on a warm, dark shelf. Keep them closed.
flow.parent: In a warm Indian kitchen, spots often show by day 2 or 3. In a cool room, below about 20 degrees, it can take up to a week. If no slice has a spot on day 4, wait up to day 7 before you decide. Keep the boxes closed the whole time.
flow.wait: Leave the boxes for two days.

flow.do: 1. Look at each slice through the lid, without opening it. 2. Count the spots on each slice. 3. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Look through the lids. Count the spots on each slice. Don't open the boxes.
flow.kid: Look through the lids. Count the spots on each slice. Keep the boxes shut.

ask.q: Which slice has the most spots so far?
good: The soil slice.
The finger slice has some spots where my fingers were.

flow.parent: If you used katoris, lift the plate only a little, look quickly, and put it back. Count shiny dots and fuzzy patches as spots.
flow.wait: Look again tomorrow, and the day after.

flow.do: 1. On day 4, count the spots one last time. 2. Look closely with a magnifying glass or the phone zoom, through the lid. 3. Draw all three slices. 4. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: So, did your fingers and the soil carry microbes? Tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Did your fingers carry microbes? Say what you think. Say what you saw. Say why.

ask.q: Why did the finger slice and the soil slice grow spots?
good: Because microbes were on my fingers and in the soil, and they multiplied on the potato.
Because each spot grew from a few microbes we could not see.

ask.q: Why did the slice nobody touched grow the fewest spots?
good: Because nothing touched it, so only a few microbes from the air got in.
Because it was closed straight away.

flow.parent: Usually the soil slice grows the most spots, in many colours, often with grey or green fuzz. The finger slice grows spots near where the fingers pressed. The Nobody slice grows the fewest: maybe none, maybe one or two from the air. A spot on the Nobody slice is not a failure. It shows that microbes float in the air too.

check.q: The finger slice grew spots. The slice nobody touched grew almost none. What does this show?
check.why: All three slices came from the same potato and sat in the same kind of box. Only the finger slice was touched by fingers, and that one grew spots. So the microbes came from the fingers. If potatoes made spots by themselves, the Nobody slice would have as many.

flow.do: 1. Do not open the boxes. 2. Put all three closed boxes in a plastic bag. 3. Tie the bag shut and put it in the bin. 4. Wash hands with soap.
flow.say: We never open these boxes now. The spots are millions of microbes. I will tie them in a bag and throw them away.
flow.kid: A grown-up throws the closed boxes away in a tied bag. Wash your hands.
flow.parent: Throw the boxes away rather than washing them. If you used steel katoris, a grown-up tips each slice into a bag outdoors, ties the bag, and then washes the katori with soap and hot water.

setup.caption: 1. Cut three slices of boiled potato and put one in each box.

setup.art: A child pressing three fingertips on one potato slice, and sprinkling a tiny pinch of soil from a flower pot on another.
setup.caption: 2. Fingers touch one slice. Soil goes on another. Nobody touches the third.

experiments.title: A Spoon, a Drop or Nothing: how much curd sets the milk?
experiments.context: In this experiment you set up three katoris of warm milk. One gets a spoon of curd, one gets only a drop, and one gets nothing. The next morning you see which ones turned into curd. This shows whether a few curd bacteria can multiply enough to set a whole katori.
experiments.question: A spoon of curd sets a bowl of milk. Would just one drop of curd be enough?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which katoris will turn into curd by morning: the spoon one, the drop one, the one with nothing, or more than one? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three katoris get the same milk, the same amount, at the same warmth, in the same place, for the same time. Only the amount of curd is different. So any difference in the morning comes from how much curd went in.
results_table: Next morning: thick, a bit thick, or runny?

materials.item: milk, boiled and cooled until it feels warm on your finger, like a bath
materials.qty: about one and a half cups

materials.item: fresh plain curd from home or a shop, as the starter
three steel katoris or small bowls, the same size, with plates to cover them
a teaspoon and a toothpick or the handle of a clean spoon
three paper labels and a pen: Spoon, Drop, Nothing

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the milk and checks that the milk is warm, not hot, before a child touches the katoris.

schedule.what: In the evening, pour warm milk into three katoris. Add a spoon of curd to one, a drop to one and nothing to one. Guess which ones will turn into curd. Cover and leave in a warm place.
In the morning, tip each katori a little. Which ones set? Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Draw the three katoris from the side in the morning. Show the curd as thick, a bit thick or runny.

flow.do: 1. Boil the milk and let it cool until it feels warm, like bath water, on a clean finger. 2. Pour the same amount into each of the three katoris. 3. Label them Spoon, Drop and Nothing.
flow.say: This milk is warm, like a bath. Curd bacteria work best in warm milk. We have three katoris with the same milk.
flow.kid: Look at the three katoris of warm milk. They are all the same.
flow.parent: Milk that is too hot can kill the curd bacteria. Warm enough to keep a finger in for ten seconds is right.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason for each katori. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: One katori gets a spoon of curd. One gets just one drop. One gets nothing. Which will be curd by morning? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One gets a spoon of curd. One gets one drop. One gets nothing. Which will be curd? Why?

ask.q: Will one drop of curd be enough?
good: No, a drop is too little.
Yes, because the bacteria will multiply.
Maybe, but slower.

flow.parent: Every guess is fine, as long as there is a reason.

flow.do: 1. Stir one teaspoon of curd into the Spoon katori. 2. Dip the tip of a toothpick in the curd, and stir that tiny drop into the Drop katori. 3. Add nothing to the Nothing katori. 4. Cover all three with plates.
flow.say: A whole spoon of curd goes into this one. Just a drop on the toothpick goes into this one. Nothing goes into the last one. Now we put the plates on.
flow.kid: Stir a spoon of curd into one. Stir a toothpick drop into one. Add nothing to the last. Cover them.
flow.parent: Use a clean toothpick or spoon handle, so that the drop is the only curd that goes in.

flow.do: 1. Put the three covered katoris in a warm place, such as a closed cupboard or a closed casserole. 2. Leave them overnight, about 8 to 10 hours. Don't stir or move them.
flow.say: The bacteria need a quiet, warm night. We look in the morning.
flow.kid: Put the katoris in a warm place. Leave them all night.
flow.parent: In cold weather, wrap the katoris in a towel or put them in a closed casserole, so that they stay warm.

flow.do: 1. In the morning, lift each plate. 2. Tip each katori a little to the side. 3. Let your child gently touch the top with a clean spoon.
flow.say: Tip each katori a little. Is the milk thick and set, a bit thick, or still runny?
flow.kid: Tip each katori a little. Is it thick, a bit thick, or runny?

ask.q: What happened in each katori?
good: The spoon one is thick curd.
The drop one set too, but it is softer.
The nothing one is still milk.

flow.parent: Usually the Spoon katori is firm curd. The Drop katori often sets too, but softer, or needs a few more hours. The Nothing katori stays runny milk. In very hot weather, the milk in the Nothing katori can turn sour and lumpy by the next day, but it does not set smooth and firm. If the Drop katori is still runny, leave it covered for 4 more hours and look again.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why. Then let them taste a little of the Spoon curd, if it is fresh.
flow.say: So, was one drop enough? Tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Was one drop enough? Say what you think. Say what you saw. Say why.

ask.q: How could one drop set a whole katori?
good: Because the few bacteria in the drop multiplied all night.
Because they split into two again and again until there were millions.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the evidence: the drop katori set, the nothing katori did not, so the curd bacteria in the drop must have multiplied. Do not let anyone taste the Nothing katori.

check.q: Suppose the Drop katori set into curd, but the Nothing katori stayed runny. Why?
options: The drop had a few curd bacteria, and they multiplied all night
The plate made the milk thick
Milk always turns into curd by itself
check.why: All three katoris had a plate and warm milk. The Nothing katori stayed runny, so milk does not set into curd by itself. The drop carried a few curd bacteria, and by morning they had multiplied into millions.

activities.title: Smell the Soil: a smell made by bacteria
activities.context: In this activity you smell dry soil from a flower pot, then sprinkle water on it and smell again. Much of the earthy smell you notice is made by bacteria that live in the soil. This is the smell people love after the first rain.

materials.item: a flower pot with dry soil on top, or two spoons of dry soil in a steel bowl
a cup of water, or a small spray bottle

schedule.what: Smell dry soil. Sprinkle water. Smell again. Talk about who made the smell.

activities.record: Draw the flower pot. Draw the smell rising from the wet soil, and draw a few tiny bacteria in the soil.

flow.do: 1. Choose a pot whose top soil is dry. 2. Ask your child to bend close and smell the dry soil.
flow.say: Smell the dry soil. Does it have much of a smell?
flow.kid: Bend close to the dry soil. Smell it. Does it have much of a smell?

ask.q: What does the dry soil smell like?
good: Not much.
A little dusty.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason before adding water.
flow.say: We will sprinkle water on the soil. Will the smell change? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Water goes on the soil next. Will the smell change? Why?

ask.q: Will the smell change?
good: Yes, it will smell like rain.
No, water has no smell.

flow.do: 1. Sprinkle a little water over the soil, like the first drops of rain. 2. Wait ten seconds. 3. Smell again.
flow.say: Sprinkle the water gently, like the first rain. Now smell again. What changed?
flow.kid: Sprinkle the water like rain. Wait a moment. Smell again. What changed?

ask.q: What does the wet soil smell like?
good: Like the first rain.
Earthy, like a garden.

flow.parent: The earthy smell comes mostly from a substance called geosmin. Soil bacteria make geosmin. Rain and sprinkled water lift tiny amounts into the air. Human noses can smell geosmin even when there is very, very little. If the soil has very little smell, try a dry clay diya or matka, which often smells earthy when wet.

flow.do: Tell your child who makes the smell. Then wash hands.
flow.say: Tiny bacteria in the soil make much of that smell. In 1964, Isabel Joy Bear, a scientist in Australia, and her colleague Richard Thomas named the rain smell petrichor. In Kannauj, perfume makers make a scent called mitti attar from baked earth.
flow.kid: Bacteria in the soil make much of that smell. You smelled something made by microbes. Wash your hands now.

ask.q: Who made the earthy smell?
good: Tiny bacteria in the soil.
Microbes.

check.q: Much of the earthy smell of wet soil is made by whom?
check.why: Soil bacteria make a substance called geosmin. Water lifts tiny amounts into the air, and our noses pick it up. Clouds and pots do not make the smell.

setup.art: A child bending close to a flower pot of dry soil on a balcony, sniffing.
setup.caption: 1. Smell the dry soil.

setup.art: A hand sprinkling water from a cup over the soil, with small wavy smell lines rising from the wet patches.
setup.caption: 2. Sprinkle water like rain, wait, and smell again.

activities.title: Microbe Map of Our Flat
activities.context: In this activity you walk through your home and mark every place where microbes live. Then you count your marks. You will find that microbes live almost everywhere.

materials.item: a big sheet of paper or the back of an old calendar
pencils or crayons, and small round stickers or a red crayon for dots

schedule.what: Draw a simple map of the home. Walk round and put a dot wherever microbes live. Count the dots.

activities.record: The map itself, with a dot at every place, and the total number of dots written at the bottom.

flow.do: Help your child draw a simple map of the home: one box for each room, the balcony and the kitchen.
flow.say: Let's draw our home from above, like a bird flying over the roof. One box for each room.
flow.kid: Draw your home from above. Draw a box for each room.
flow.parent: It does not have to be neat. Boxes and labels are enough.

flow.do: 1. Walk from room to room together. 2. At each place, ask: do microbes live here? 3. Put a dot on the map for each yes.
flow.say: Do microbes live on the door handle? In the flower pot? In the curd? On the pillow? Put a dot for each place.
flow.kid: Walk round your home. Put a dot where microbes live.

ask.q: Can you find a place in our home with no microbes at all?
good: The inside of a sealed new tin of food.
Water that has just boiled.
I could not find one.

flow.parent: Good places to check: door handles, the tap, the sponge, the flower pots, the curd, the idli or dosa batter, the dustbin, the pillow, the toothbrush, the pet's bowl, and your own hands and mouth. Almost no place is free of microbes. A sealed tin of food and water that has just boiled have almost none alive.

flow.do: Count the dots together and write the number at the bottom of the map.
flow.say: How many dots did you put? Is there any room with no dots?
flow.kid: Count your dots. Write the number at the bottom.

ask.q: Which room has the most dots?
good: The kitchen, because there is food.
The bathroom, because it is damp.

setup.art: A child drawing a simple map of a flat on a big sheet of paper, with boxes for the kitchen, a bedroom, a bathroom and a balcony.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a map of your home.

setup.art: The same map covered with red dots at the door handle, the tap, a flower pot, a katori of curd and a toothbrush.
setup.caption: 2. Put a dot wherever microbes live, then count the dots.

activities.title: How Small? Microbes in a full stop
activities.context: In this activity you draw the smallest dot you can, and compare it with a mustard seed. A microbe is much smaller than either. Hundreds of bacteria could sit side by side across your tiny dot.

materials.item: a sharp pencil and a sheet of paper
a few mustard seeds (rai or kadugu)
a magnifying glass, or the zoom on a phone camera, if you have one

schedule.what: Draw the smallest dot you can. Put a mustard seed beside the dot. Talk about how many bacteria would fit across each.

activities.record: Draw your dot and a mustard seed, and write: about 300 bacteria across my dot, about 1000 across the seed.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the smallest dot they can with a sharp pencil. Put one mustard seed next to the dot.
flow.say: Draw the tiniest dot you can. Now put a mustard seed next to the dot. Which is smaller?
flow.kid: Draw the tiniest dot you can. Put a mustard seed next to the dot. Which is smaller?

ask.q: Which is smaller, the dot or the seed?
good: The dot.
The seed is a bit bigger.

flow.do: Look at both through a magnifying glass or the phone zoom. Then tell your child the numbers.
flow.say: A microbe is far smaller than your dot. About a thousand bacteria in a line would just reach across this mustard seed. A few hundred would fit across your dot.
flow.kid: A microbe is much smaller than your dot. A few hundred bacteria fit across your dot.
flow.parent: A typical bacterium is about one thousandth of a millimetre long. A mustard seed is about one millimetre across, and a fine pencil dot is about a third of a millimetre. These numbers are rough, because bacteria come in different sizes.

flow.do: Ask the question below and let your child think.
flow.say: If microbes are that small, how could we ever know they are there?
flow.kid: Microbes are too small to see. How could we know they are there?

ask.q: How could we know microbes are there?
good: Use a microscope.
Let them grow into a spot we can see, like on the potato.
See what they do, like making curd.

setup.art: A tiny pencil dot and a round mustard seed side by side on white paper.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the tiniest dot you can, next to a mustard seed.

setup.art: A magnifying glass over the dot, with a zoom circle showing a long row of tiny bacteria lined up across the dot.
setup.caption: 2. Hundreds of bacteria could line up across your dot.

activities.title: The Rising Batter (if your family makes idli or dosa batter)
activities.context: In this activity you mark the level of fresh idli or dosa batter at night and look again in the morning. Microbes in the batter make gas bubbles overnight, and the batter rises. If your family does not make batter at home, skip this one.

materials.item: fresh idli or dosa batter in its vessel, just ground
a rubber band, or a small strip of tape, to mark the level on the outside of the vessel

schedule.what: At night, mark the level of the fresh batter. Smell it. Guess what will happen.
In the morning, look at the level, the bubbles and the smell.

activities.record: Draw the vessel at night and in the morning, with the batter level and the rubber band marked.

flow.do: 1. Put a rubber band round the outside of the vessel, at the top of the batter. 2. Let your child smell the batter. 3. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: The rubber band shows where the batter is now. Smell it. What will the batter look like in the morning? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The band shows where the batter is. Smell it. What will happen by morning? Why?

ask.q: What will happen by morning?
good: It will go up.
It will stay the same.
It will smell sour.

flow.parent: Leave enough space in the vessel, because the batter can nearly double in a warm kitchen.
flow.wait: Leave the batter overnight in its usual warm place.

flow.do: 1. In the morning, look at the batter level against the rubber band. 2. Look for bubbles on top and on the sides. 3. Smell it again.
flow.say: Where is the batter now? Can you see bubbles? How does it smell?
flow.kid: Where is the batter now? Look for bubbles. Smell it again.

ask.q: Why did the batter rise?
good: Microbes made gas bubbles in the batter.
Tiny living beings were working all night.

flow.parent: Bacteria and yeasts in the batter eat some of the starch and sugar. They make gas, which lifts the batter, and acid, which makes the batter sour. Most of these microbes came in on the urad dal and rice. In cold weather the batter rises less.

setup.art: The same vessel in the morning, the batter risen well above the band, with bubbles on top.

games.title: Lots, A Few or Almost None? A card game of where microbes live
games.context: This is a card game about where microbes live. Each card names a place. You guess whether that place has lots of microbes, a few, or almost none. Then you turn the card over to check.

items.f: A spoon of curd
items.b: Lots. Millions of curd bacteria in one spoon.

items.f: A spoon of soil from a flower pot
items.b: Lots. One teaspoon of rich soil can hold about as many bacteria as there are people in India.

items.f: Your hands, after playing
items.b: Lots. Thousands of microbes, even when your hands look clean.

items.f: Inside your tummy
items.b: Lots. More microbes live in your gut than anywhere else on your body.

items.f: A spoon of sea water
items.b: Lots. One small spoon of sea water can hold millions of bacteria.

items.f: Fresh idli batter, the next morning
items.b: Lots. Microbes made the batter rise and turn sour.

items.f: Your toothbrush
items.b: Lots. Microbes from your mouth stay on the bristles.

items.f: The air in your room
items.b: A few. Microbes float on tiny bits of dust.

items.f: A cloud high in the sky
items.b: A few. Scientists have found living bacteria in clouds.

items.f: A hot spring
items.b: Lots. Thick mats of microbes grow in hot springs, in water too hot to touch.

items.f: Water that has just boiled
items.b: Almost none. Boiling kills almost all microbes.

items.f: Food inside a sealed new tin
items.b: Almost none. The food was heated after the tin was sealed, and nothing can get in.

printables.title: 12 answer cards (3 for each of up to 4 players)

rules: Each player takes three answer cards: Lots, A few and Almost none. Two players use 6 of the 12 answer cards.
Mix the 12 place cards and put them in a pile, front side up.
One player reads the top place card aloud.
Every player puts one answer card face down at the same time, then everyone turns the cards over.
Turn the place card over and read the back aloud.
Everyone who chose the right answer makes one tally mark on a sheet of paper.
Play until all 12 place cards are done. The player with the most tally marks reads first next time. If the marks are equal, everyone wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 place cards and the answer cards. 2. Give each player three answer cards. 3. Put out a sheet of paper for tally marks. 4. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Each card is a place. You guess: lots of microbes, a few, or almost none.
flow.kid: Each card is a place. Guess: lots of microbes, a few, or almost none?

flow.do: Play all 12 cards. After each card, ask the question below.
flow.say: Why do you think this place has so many microbes? Or so few?
flow.kid: Read your card. Choose your answer card. Turn the place card over.

ask.q: Why did you choose that answer?
good: Because there is food and it is warm.
Because it is very hot there.
Because boiling kills them.

flow.parent: Children are often surprised by the cloud and the hot spring. Microbes live in more places than any other kind of living being.

flow.do: Count the tally marks. Ask the last question.
flow.say: Which card surprised you most? Why?
flow.kid: Count your tally marks. Which card surprised you most?

check.q: Scientists found living bacteria in clouds high in the sky. What does this show?
options: Microbes can float in the air and live high up
check.why: Microbes float in the air on tiny bits of dust, and some have been found alive in clouds. Clouds are made of water drops, and microbes live in many places besides the sea.

setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 12 place cards and three answer cards for each player.

setup.caption: 2. Read a place, choose an answer card, then turn the place card over.

games.title: Helper or Germ? A sorting race
games.context: This is a sorting game. Each card names a microbe and what that microbe does. You sort the cards into helpers, harmless ones and germs. You will find that most microbes are not germs.

items.f: Curd bacteria: turn milk into curd
items.b: Helper

items.f: Batter microbes: make idli batter rise
items.b: Helper

items.f: Baker's yeast: makes bread dough puff up
items.b: Helper

items.f: Soil bacteria: break dead leaves into new soil
items.b: Helper

items.f: Gut bacteria: help you digest food
items.b: Helper

items.f: Root bacteria: live in lumps on moong and chana roots, and help the plant grow
items.b: Helper

items.f: Sea microbes: make oxygen from sunlight
items.b: Helper

items.f: Most skin microbes: live quietly on your skin
items.b: Harmless, and some keep germs away

items.f: Cold virus: gives you a runny nose
items.b: Germ

items.f: Cholera bacteria: spread in dirty water and cause a bad tummy illness
items.b: Germ

items.f: Mould on an old chapati: can make you sick if you eat it
items.b: Germ, if eaten

items.f: Tooth bacteria: make acid from sweets that can make holes in teeth
items.b: Germ, if teeth are not brushed

rules: Put the three sorting labels on the floor: Helper, Harmless and Germ.
Mix the 12 microbe cards and deal them out, front side up.
On your turn, read one card aloud and put the card by the label you think is right.
When all 12 cards are down, turn each one over to check. Move any card that is by the wrong label.
Count how many cards are by each label. The goal is for everyone, together, to sort all 12 cards correctly.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 microbe cards and the 3 labels. 2. Put the labels on the floor. 3. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Each card is a microbe and what that microbe does. Is the microbe a helper, harmless, or a germ?
flow.kid: Read each card. Is that microbe a helper, harmless, or a germ?

flow.do: Take turns to place the cards. Then turn them all over and check together.
flow.say: Read your card aloud. Where does the microbe go? Why?
flow.kid: Read your card. Put the card by Helper, Harmless or Germ.

ask.q: Why did you put the curd bacteria there?
good: Because they make curd for us.
Because they help.

flow.do: Count the cards by each label. Ask the question below.
flow.say: How many helpers did we find? How many germs? What does that tell us about microbes?
flow.kid: Count the cards by each label. Are most microbes germs?

ask.q: Are most microbes germs?
good: No, most are helpers or harmless.
Only a few are germs.

check.q: In the sorting game, most cards were helpers. What does that tell us?
options: Most microbes are helpful or harmless
check.why: Seven cards were helpers and one was harmless. Only four were germs. In the real world too, most microbes are helpful or harmless, and only a few are germs.

setup.caption: 1. Put the three labels down and deal the microbe cards.

setup.caption: 2. Sort every card, then turn them over and count each pile.

projects.title: The Curd Chain: one starter for a whole week
projects.context: In this week-long project you set a small katori of curd every night, using a spoon of the curd you made the night before. You keep a chart of each day's curd. The bacteria from the first spoon keep multiplying, katori after katori.

materials.item: milk, boiled and cooled until warm
materials.qty: about half a cup each night

materials.item: one spoon of plain curd, to start the chain on day 1
one steel katori with a plate to cover the katori
a sheet of paper for the chart, and a pencil

projects.safety: A grown-up warms the milk and checks that the milk is warm, not hot, before the child adds the starter.

schedule.what: Set the first katori with a spoon of curd. Draw the first ring of the chain on the chart.
Check the curd. Eat most of the curd and save one spoon. Set the next katori with that spoon.
Check the curd. Eat most of the curd and save one spoon. Set the next katori with that spoon. Add a ring to the chain on the chart.
Check the curd. Eat most of the curd and save one spoon. Set the next katori with that spoon. Add a ring to the chain on the chart.
Check the curd. Eat most of the curd and save one spoon. Set the next katori with that spoon. Add a ring to the chain on the chart.
Check the curd. Eat most of the curd and save one spoon. Set the next katori with that spoon. Add a ring to the chain on the chart.
Eat the last curd. Count the rings on the chart. Talk about where the bacteria in today's curd came from.

projects.record: A paper chain chart: one ring for each katori, with a word for the curd (thick, soft or runny) and a taste face.

flow.do: 1. Warm the milk until it feels like a bath. 2. Pour half a cup into the katori. 3. Your child stirs in one spoon of curd. 4. Cover and leave in a warm place overnight. 5. Draw the first ring on the chart.
flow.say: This spoon of curd starts our chain. Tomorrow we will use a spoon of this new curd to make the next one.
flow.kid: Stir in the spoon of curd. Cover the katori. Draw the first ring on your chart.
flow.parent: Warm milk is enough: if you can keep a clean finger in it for ten seconds, it is right. In cold weather, wrap the katori in a towel.

flow.do: Each day: 1. Check the curd and write one word on the chart. 2. Eat most of it with a meal. 3. Save one spoon. 4. Use that spoon to set the next katori.
flow.say: Is today's curd thick? Save one spoon. That spoon carries the bacteria into tomorrow's curd.
flow.kid: Is the curd thick? Write it on the chart. Save one spoon for tomorrow.

ask.q: Where did the bacteria in today's curd come from?
good: From yesterday's spoon.
From the very first spoon, again and again.

flow.parent: Put the saved spoon of curd in a clean cup, then rinse the katori with hot water and set the next katori. If one day's curd is runny or smells bad, start again with fresh curd from the shop.

flow.do: On day 7, eat the last curd and count the rings. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Our chain has six rings. The bacteria in today's curd came from the very first spoon, passed from katori to katori. How many times did a spoon from one katori go into the next?
flow.kid: Count the rings. How many times did a spoon move bacteria into the next katori?

ask.q: How many times did a spoon from one katori go into the next?
good: Five times.
Every night from day 2 to day 6.

flow.parent: Six katoris were set, one each night for six nights. The first spoon came from outside, so a saved spoon went into the next katori five times. Many families in India keep a curd going for years, sharing a spoon of starter with neighbours.

setup.art: A paper chart with six rings joined in a chain, each with a word like thick or soft and a little face.

challenges.title: Keep the Slice Clean
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the Three Potato Slices experiment, spots grew on a boiled potato slice in a few days. Now you invent a way to keep a slice free of spots for as long as you can.
challenges.problem: Spots grow on a boiled potato slice in a few days in a warm kitchen. How could you keep a slice without spots for the longest time, using only things from home?
constraints: The slice must stay in a closed box, so you never need to open it to check.
Test your idea against a plain slice in a box, so you can compare.
materials: a boiled potato and a clean knife, for the grown-up
small clear boxes with lids, or zip bags
things from the kitchen, such as salt, lemon, turmeric or a place in the fridge
general: Keep the slice in the fridge, where it is cold and microbes multiply slowly.
Close the box the moment the slice goes in, so fewer microbes land on the slice.
Pat the slice dry with a clean tissue before closing the box, because most microbes need water to grow.
creative: Cover the slice in salt, the way pickles keep, because salt pulls water out of microbes.
Squeeze lemon juice on the slice, because many microbes grow slowly in sour food.
Dust the slice with turmeric, and see whether turmeric slows the spots down.
challenges.your_turn: Choose your own way to keep a slice clean. Set up your slice and a plain slice today. Count the spots on both every day for four days.

flow.do: Read the problem to your child. Ask for ideas before showing any.
flow.say: Spots grow fast on a boiled potato. How could we keep a slice clean for the longest time?
flow.kid: Spots grow fast on a potato slice. How can you keep a slice clean?

ask.q: What ideas do you have?
good: Put the slice in the fridge.
Put salt on the slice.
Close the box quickly.

flow.do: 1. Read out the usual and creative ideas. 2. Your child picks one. 3. The grown-up cuts two slices. 4. Set up one slice with the idea and one plain slice, each in a closed box.
flow.say: Which idea will you test? We need a plain slice too, so we can compare.
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Set up your slice and a plain slice. Close both boxes.
flow.parent: If the idea is the fridge, keep the plain slice on the kitchen shelf.

flow.do: For four days, count the spots on both slices through the lid. On day 4, compare. A grown-up throws the closed boxes away.
flow.say: Which slice has fewer spots? Did your idea work? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count the spots on both slices. Did your idea work? Why?

ask.q: Did your idea keep the slice cleaner?
good: Yes, the fridge slice had no spots.
No, both slices grew spots.

flow.parent: Cold, salt and dryness usually slow spots the most. An idea that does not work is still a good result, because now you know.
flow.wait: Count the spots each day for four days.

setup.caption: 1. Set up your idea next to a plain slice.

setup.art: The same two boxes after four days: the plain slice spotty, the salted slice almost clean.

items.p: Draw a line from each place to the microbes that live there.
pairs: Wet soil in a flower pot
Bacteria that make the rain smell
items.why: Microbes live in all these places. Curd bacteria set milk, soil bacteria make the rain smell, and thousands of microbes live on our hands.

items.p: What is a microbe?
opts: A living being too small to see
items.why: A microbe is a living being too small to see with our eyes alone. Most microbes are a single cell. A tiny stone is not alive, and a baby ant is big enough to see.

items.p: A hand that looks clean has no microbes on it.
items.why: False. In the Three Potato Slices experiment, the slice touched by fingers grew spots. Microbes live on hands even when the hands look clean.

items.p: Draw the three potato slices from the Three Potato Slices experiment as they looked on the last day. Draw every spot you saw.
items.art: Three empty slice outlines in a row, labelled Soil, Fingers and Nobody.
items.a: Three slices. The soil slice has the most spots, the finger slice has some spots near the fingerprints, and the Nobody slice has the fewest.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the spots in their colours and labels each slice. The drawing shows that soil and fingers carried microbes.

items.p: Look at the picture. The soil slice has 9 spots. The finger slice has 4 spots. How many more spots does the soil slice have?
items.art: Two potato slices: one with 9 coloured spots, one with 4 round spots.
items.why: 9 take away 4 is 5. The soil slice has 5 more spots, because soil carries even more microbes than fingers.

items.p: Each spot on the potato is a crowd of millions of microbes. A spot like this is called a ________.
items.why: A colony is a spot of microbes that grew from one or a few. We can see a colony even though each microbe is too small to see.

items.p: Why did the slice nobody touched grow the fewest spots? Write one or two sentences.
items.a: Nothing touched it, so only a few microbes from the air landed on it.
items.why: A strong answer says that the spots come from microbes that land on the slice, and fewer microbes reached the slice that nobody touched.

items.p: Three of these are full of microbes. Which one has almost none?
items.why: Curd, soil and hands all carry many microbes. Water that has just boiled has almost none alive, because boiling kills them.

items.p: Label the picture of the kitchen. Write curd, soil, hands or air next to each place where microbes live.
items.art: A simple kitchen with a katori of curd on a shelf, a flower pot by a window, a child washing hands, and arrows pointing to each place and to the open window.
items.a: Curd: the katori on the shelf. Soil: the flower pot by the window. Hands: the child's hands. Air: the space by the open window.
items.why: Microbes live in all four places. A strong answer labels all four and knows that the air holds microbes too.

items.p: Why do we wash our hands with soap before we eat?
opts: Soap washes off most germs before they get inside us
Soap kills every microbe on Earth
items.why: A few microbes are germs, and soap and water wash most of them off our hands. Soap does not kill every microbe, and most microbes are not harmful.

items.p: Two sisters in Hyderabad look at a potato slice with spots on it after four days in a closed box.

views.says: The spots came out of the potato. Old food makes spots by itself.
The spots came from microbes that landed on the potato. The potato was just their food.

items.ask: Which sister do you agree with more? Give a reason from the potato test. Then say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees more with Ayesha and uses the test: the slice nobody touched grew the fewest spots, so the spots came from what touched the slices. Zara has something right too: the potato is the food that the microbes grew on.
items.why: The spots are colonies grown from microbes that landed on the slice. The potato only gave them food. A strong answer uses the Nobody slice as evidence.

items.p: Why did the soil slice grow the most spots?
opts: Soil holds a huge number of microbes
items.why: Soil is packed with microbes. One teaspoon of rich soil can hold about as many bacteria as there are people in India. So a pinch of soil put many more microbes on the slice than fingers did.

items.p: Put these in order, to show how a spot grows.
items: Millions make a spot we can see
A few microbes land on the potato
a: A few microbes land on the potato
Millions make a spot we can see
items.why: Spots grow because microbes multiply. Each one splits into two, again and again, until there are enough to see.

items.p: One bacterium splits into 2. Each of those splits, making 4. Each of those splits again. How many bacteria are there now?
items.why: Each split doubles the number. 1 becomes 2, 2 becomes 4, and 4 becomes 8.

items.p: Draw what you think one spot on the potato looks like through a very strong microscope.
items.art: A big empty circle, like the view through a microscope.
items.a: Many tiny cells packed together, round or rod-shaped, or long thin threads for mould.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that a spot is made of many tiny cells crowded together. A child who draws threads for a fuzzy spot has understood that mould grows threads.

items.p: Curd sets faster in a cold room than in a warm room.
items.why: False. Curd bacteria multiply fastest in warm milk. In the cold they work slowly, so the milk sets slowly.

items.p: You want to set curd tonight. You have warm milk, but no curd. Write what you could do.
items.a: Ask a neighbour for one spoon of curd, or buy a little plain curd, and stir it into the warm milk.
items.why: A strong answer knows that curd needs a starter with living curd bacteria. Without the bacteria, the milk will not set into smooth curd.

items.p: Match each thing to the microbe job.
pairs: Bacteria make the milk sour and thick
items.why: Each of these foods and smells is made by microbes at work.

items.p: When a microbe splits into two, and two into four, we say the microbes ________.
items.why: To multiply means to become many. Microbes multiply by splitting.

items.p: Label the three katoris from the experiment A Spoon, a Drop or Nothing: thick curd, soft curd, runny milk. Then write what went into each.
items.art: Three katoris tipped a little: one firm, one soft, one runny.
items.a: Spoon: thick curd. Drop: soft curd. Nothing: runny milk.
items.why: The Spoon katori got the most curd bacteria, so that katori set firmest. The drop had only a few, so it set softer or slower. The katori with nothing stayed milk.

items.p: Three people talk about the microbes in a home.

views.says: Kill 99 percent of germs on every surface, every day.

views.who: A grandmother who keeps curd and pickles
views.says: Microbes made my curd and my idli. Most of them are friends.

views.who: Dr Lakshmi, a children's doctor in Madurai
views.says: Wash hands with soap before eating and after the toilet. You don't need to clean every surface all day.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say what one of the others has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one view and gives a reason, then answers back from another view. For example: Dr Lakshmi is right that soap removes germs before meals, but the grandmother is right that most microbes are helpful, so there is no need to kill them everywhere.
items.why: All three have part of the truth. Most microbes are helpful or harmless, a few are germs, and soap at the right times removes most germs. Scientists are still studying whether meeting many harmless microbes protects children from allergies.

items.p: A friend says, 'I can't see any microbes, so they are not real.' Write what you would show your friend to change their mind.
items.a: I would show my friend the potato slices, where spots grew from fingers, or set curd with one drop of curd.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence a friend can see: the spots that grow from fingers or soil, or curd that sets from a drop. We can see what microbes do, and the crowds they make.

items.p: Suppose you do the Three Potato Slices experiment again. This time you wash your hands with soap before pressing your fingers on the slice. What will probably happen?
items.why: Soap and water wash most microbes off hands. So the slice should grow fewer spots than before, but maybe not zero, because a few microbes stay on skin.

items.p: In the curd experiment, one katori of warm milk got a spoon of curd and one got only a drop. Suppose the Drop katori set softer than the Spoon katori. Why would that happen?
items.a: The drop had fewer curd bacteria, so they took longer to multiply and set the milk.
items.why: A strong answer links the amount of starter to the number of bacteria, and the number of bacteria to how fast the milk sets.

items.p: Put these in order, from the most microbes to the fewest, as in the potato test.
items.why: Soil holds the most microbes, fingers carry many, and the slice nobody touched only got a few from the air.

items.p: Microbes lived on Earth long before there were any animals.
items.why: True. Microbes have lived on Earth for at least 3.5 billion years. The first animals came much later.

items.p: Draw a map of your body. Put dots where microbes live: skin, mouth, tummy and anywhere else you think.
items.art: A simple outline of a child's body, front view.
items.a: A body outline with dots on the skin, in the mouth, in the tummy and on the hands.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the most dots in the tummy, where most of the body's microbes live, and some on skin, hands and in the mouth.

items.p: After the curd sets, many families keep it in the fridge. Why does the curd stay fresh longer there?
items.a: It is cold in the fridge, so the curd bacteria multiply slowly and the curd turns sour more slowly.
items.why: A strong answer says microbes multiply slowly in the cold. This is why a fridge keeps food fresh longer.

items.p: In the curd chain, suppose you set a new katori of curd every night for 6 nights. Then you share one spoon with each of 3 neighbours, and each neighbour sets one katori. How many katoris of curd came from your first spoon?
items.why: 6 katoris at home and 3 at the neighbours' homes. 6 and 3 make 9. All of them carry bacteria from the first spoon.

items.p: Label the picture of a fuzzy spot on bread. Write: thread, spot, bread.
items.art: A close-up of a slice of bread with one round fuzzy mould patch, thin threads spreading at the edge of the patch.
items.a: Thread: the thin lines at the edge. Spot: the round fuzzy patch. Bread: the slice underneath.
items.why: Mould is a fungus that grows by spreading thin threads. A strong answer labels the threads at the edge, where the mould is growing outwards.

quiz.p: Why can't we see one microbe with our eyes?
opts: Microbes only come out at night
quiz.why: Microbes are much smaller than the smallest thing our eyes can see. A thousand bacteria in a row would just reach across a mustard seed.

opts: Almost everywhere: on skin, in soil, air, water and food
quiz.why: Microbes live almost everywhere on Earth. Even clean-looking hands carry thousands.

quiz.p: A spot on the potato is too big to be one microbe. What is a spot?
opts: A crowd of millions of microbes
quiz.why: Each spot is a colony: millions of microbes that grew from one or a few by splitting again and again.

quiz.p: What do curd bacteria do to milk?
opts: Eat the milk sugar and make the milk thick and sour
quiz.why: Curd bacteria eat the sugar in milk and make an acid. That acid makes the milk thick and sour.

quiz.p: Why do we add a spoon of old curd to warm milk?
opts: To add the living curd bacteria
quiz.why: The spoon of curd is the starter. The starter carries the living bacteria that turn the milk into curd.
Most microbes are harmless or helpful. Only a few are germs.

quiz.p: Who makes much of the earthy smell when rain falls on dry soil?
quiz.why: Soil bacteria make a substance called geosmin. Rain lifts tiny amounts into the air, and we smell it.

quiz.p: You press unwashed fingers on one potato slice. You put a second slice in a box without touching it. Why do you need the second slice?
opts: To compare, so you know the spots came from your fingers
quiz.why: The untouched slice shows what grows without fingers. If only the finger slice grows many spots, the spots must have come from the fingers. This makes the test fair.

quiz.p: Where do spots on old food come from?
opts: From microbes that land on the food and multiply
From the light in the room
quiz.why: Spots come from microbes that land on the food. Louis Pasteur showed that boiled soup kept away from dust and air did not spoil.

quiz.p: Why does a tiny spoon of curd set a whole katori of warm milk overnight?
opts: The bacteria in the spoon multiply into millions
The spoon makes the milk cold
quiz.why: The few curd bacteria in the spoon split again and again all night. By morning there are millions, enough to turn the whole katori into curd.

applications: Families all over India set curd every day with a spoon of starter.
Idli, dosa, dhokla and appam batters rise because microbes make gas in them.
Farmers and gardeners keep soil healthy, because soil microbes turn dead leaves into food for plants.
Doctors grow microbes from a sick person's sample to find out which germ is causing the illness.
Fridges keep food fresh longer, because microbes multiply slowly in the cold.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of microbes are there on Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have named only a small part of them. Most kinds have never been grown in a laboratory, so we know them only from bits of their DNA. Guesses range from millions of kinds to far more.

open_questions.q: Do the microbes in curd stay and live in our tummy?
open_questions.why_open: Some curd bacteria are killed by stomach acid, and some get through. Scientists are still studying how long they stay and what they do there.

ask_kids: Where do you think microbes are living right now, in this room?
If you could shrink to the size of a microbe, where would you like to live?
Why do you think we keep curd in the fridge after it sets?
What would happen to the dead leaves in a park if there were no microbes?
Do you think the microbes on your hands are the same kinds as the ones in the soil? How could you find out?
Why do many families save a spoon of curd every day?

jokes.j: Why did the microbe cross the microscope?
jokes.a: To get to the other slide.

jokes.j: What did the curd say to the milk?
jokes.a: Don't worry, you'll set in by morning.

jokes.j: Why are bacteria so good at maths?
What do you call a mould that tells jokes?
Why did the yeast go to the party?
Why is soil so popular with microbes?
jokes.a: Because it is the most down-to-earth place to live.
Because it is full of culture.

jokes.j: Why was the idli batter so happy?
jokes.a: Because it was on the rise.

maths.problem: In the potato test, the soil slice grew 12 spots, the finger slice grew 5 spots and the Nobody slice grew 1 spot. How many spots grew on all three slices together?
maths.explain: 12 and 5 make 17. 17 and 1 make 18. So 18 spots grew on all three slices.
maths.context: This is about the spots you counted in the potato test.
maths.why_maths: Adding the spots tells us how many colonies grew in the whole test.

maths.problem: On day 2 the soil slice had 3 spots. On day 3 it had 8 spots. On day 4 it had 12 spots. On which day did the most new spots appear?
maths.explain: From day 2 to day 3, the spots went from 3 to 8, which is 5 new spots. From day 3 to day 4, they went from 8 to 12, which is 4 new spots. 5 is more than 4, so day 3 had the most new spots.
maths.context: This is about counting spots each day in the potato test.
maths.why_maths: Finding the new spots each day shows when the microbes were growing fastest.

maths.problem: One bacterium splits into 2. Each new one splits too, every half hour. How many bacteria are there after 4 splits?
maths.explain: 1 becomes 2, 2 becomes 4, 4 becomes 8, and 8 becomes 16. Each split doubles the number.
maths.context: This is about how one microbe becomes a spot you can see.
maths.why_maths: The doubling pattern shows why a few microbes can become millions overnight.

maths.problem: Each night of the curd chain uses half a cup of milk. How many cups of milk do 6 nights use?
maths.explain: Two nights use one cup, because two halves make one whole. 6 nights is three lots of two nights. So 6 nights use 3 cups.
maths.context: This is about the milk used in the curd chain project.
maths.why_maths: Working out the milk helps a family plan the curd chain for a week.
