founder: ideas/by_topic/microorganisms.md was read. Its picture book of the first microbes (the prokaryote mother who splits into her daughters, bacteria that sense, share and signal with chemicals) shaped the splitting idea, the thread in roots and the card on microbes sensing and deciding. Its fuller evolution story suits the higher levels. The ACCURACY.md note that the maze-solver is a slime mould, not a bacterium, was followed: no maze claim is made.
science: Boiled potato slices as a growth surface for bacterial colonies: Joseph Schroeter (1872) and Robert Koch (about 1881) grew colonies on cut potato before agar came into use.
Fanny Angelina Hesse suggested agar as a solid medium for bacteria in 1881, in the laboratory of her husband Walther Hesse, who worked with Robert Koch.
Louis Pasteur's swan-necked flask experiments, about 1859 to 1862, against spontaneous generation.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's letters to the Royal Society: 'animalcules' in water (1676) and in dental plaque (1683).
Lactic acid bacteria (such as Lactobacillus and Streptococcus thermophilus) ferment lactose to lactic acid, which lowers the pH and makes the milk protein casein coagulate.

I. J. Bear and R. G. Thomas, 'Nature of argillaceous odour', Nature, 1964, naming petrichor. Geosmin, the main earthy odour, is made by Streptomyces and other soil bacteria, and humans can smell geosmin at a few parts per trillion.
A gram of fertile soil holds roughly 100 million to over a billion bacteria.
Sender, Fuchs and Milo, 2016: about 1.3 bacterial cells for every human cell in the body, most of them in the gut.
Bacterial chemotaxis, and quorum sensing in Vibrio species (Bonnie Bassler and others).
Marine phytoplankton, including cyanobacteria, carry out about half of Earth's photosynthesis.
Idli batter fermentation by lactic acid bacteria (notably Leuconostoc mesenteroides) and yeasts, carried mostly on the urad dal and rice.
Living bacteria in cloud water (for example Amato and others, studies at Puy de Dome, France). Microbes in subglacial Lake Whillans, Antarctica (Christner and others, Nature, 2014).
Lower allergy rates in children raised on traditional farms (for example Stein and others, New England Journal of Medicine, 2016).
Mitti attar, distilled from baked clay, is made in Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh.
Jain teaching on one-sensed beings in earth, water and air: Tattvartha Sutra, chapter 2. Chandogya Upanishad 6.12, the banyan seed.

roots.context: We have been growing microbes on potato slices and in milk. Now we ask what the smallest living beings tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Three Potato Slices experiment, all three slices looked clean on day one. By day four, the soil and finger slices had spots, and the untouched slice had the fewest. Each spot grew from microbes too small to see. So a hand can look clean and still carry many living beings.
deep_truth.habit: We decide what is alive, and what is clean, by what our eyes can see. Our eyes miss most of the living beings on Earth, so how a thing looks tells us little about who lives on it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Three Potato Slices experiment, spots grew where fingers and soil had touched the boiled potato, and the fewest grew where nothing touched it. In the curd experiment, one drop of curd, holding bacteria nobody could see, set a whole katori of milk overnight.

three.who_am_i: You are one person, and you are also home to millions of tiny living beings on your skin and in your tummy.
three.what_is_life: Most living beings on Earth are too small to see. Life is mostly tiny.
three.what_is_this_world: Every handle, pot of soil and katori of curd around you is full of living beings.

roots.thread: Microbes were the first life on Earth, and for billions of years they were all the life there was. Every plant and animal, you too, came from that tiny life. So the microbes on your hands are not strangers. They are relatives who stayed small, and they live everywhere the rest of us live.

teachings.teaching: Jain teachers taught that the world is full of living beings, many too small to see. Some live in earth, water and air, and have only the sense of touch. So Jain monks and nuns sweep gently and filter their water, to avoid harming them.
teachings.link: Jain thinkers noticed life where eyes cannot see it, long before microscopes. Our potato slices also showed life in soil, on fingers and in the air that no eye could see.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to break open a seed of the banyan fruit. 'What do you see?' 'Nothing at all.' Uddalaka says that the great banyan tree grows from this tiny thing that his son cannot see.
teachings.link: We could not see the microbes on our fingers either. Yet from them, big spots grew on the potato. What is too small to see can still be alive and grow into something big.

science.text: Microbes have lived on Earth for at least 3.5 billion years, far longer than any plant or animal.
Scientists' best count is that your body holds about as many bacteria as your own cells, most of them in your gut.

other_view.view: Many biologists say a microbe is a single cell that reacts to chemicals the way a thermostat reacts to heat. They say microbes are alive and busy, but that sensing and reacting is not thinking or feeling.

practice.title: Hello to the tiny ones
practice.say: Sit still and open your hands in your lap. Look at your palms. They look empty. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out slowly onto your palms. Feel the warm air. Thousands of tiny living beings live on your hands. Sit quietly with them for three breaths.
practice.kid: Sit still. Open your hands. Look at your palms. Breathe out slowly on them. Thousands of tiny beings live there. Sit quietly for three breaths.

ask: If most living beings are too small to see, what else might we be missing around us?
Uddalaka's son saw nothing inside the seed. When we cannot see anything in a place, is that place always empty?
